Letter of May 17, 1972, to the State Clearinghouse from Assistant Executive Director of the Florida Audubon Society.
Comment: "At what point does the population of a species reach a point of no return?"
Response: The answer to this may be answered academic. We are compelled by limited resources to focus our salvage efforts on species most immediately threatened with extinction. Determination of which species deserve such attention must be guided by a combination of factors including size of the remnant population and its distribution; population trends at the time; and nature of the circumstances that threaten the existence of the species.

Therefore, no one can predict that threshold in terms of numbers of individuals.

Comment: The draft statement fails to go into detail regarding the enforcement of the Endangered Species Act, as proposed. "How many convictions have the three enforcement officers in Florida obtained since the (original) Act was passed?"
Response: There are six enforcement officers of the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife in Florida including two at the Miami airport to enforce importation laws of the Endangered Species Conservation Act. Present authority under the Act does not provide for the Secretary to grant permits to import, for up to one year after listing of the species, an endangered animal the contract for which was consummated prior to the listing of the species by the Secretary. Inclusion of this provision is to assure that economic claims against the act can be dealt with on a case to case basis. The Secretary is under no obligation to grant any or all appeals made to him under the "Hardship Clause." While the provision was intended originally to apply only to importations, it is written in the proposed legislation to apply to other proposed legislation
